title: Cloud Fundamentals and Cost
summary: How the cloud is organized into regions and zones, what IaaS, PaaS and serverless trade away, and how to estimate a cloud bill (including the egress surprise).

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a **region** and an **availability zone**, and why do production systems usually run in more than one AZ?
questions.hint: Think about geography, independent failures and network latency.
keyPoints: A region is a separate geographic area; regions are isolated from each other
An AZ is one or more physically separate data centers inside a region with independent power, cooling and networking
AZs in a region are connected by low-latency links (around 1–2 ms), so synchronous replication between them is practical
Spreading across 2–3 AZs survives a data-center-level failure, which is far more common than a full region outage

questions.prompt: Explain IaaS, PaaS and serverless (FaaS). For a new team of three engineers building a web app, which would you pick for the API and the database, and why?
questions.hint: Who patches the OS? Who handles scaling and failover? What do you give up?
keyPoints: IaaS: you rent VMs and manage OS, runtime and app; most control and most operational work
PaaS: you deploy app code and the platform handles OS, runtime and scaling
Serverless/FaaS: you deploy functions billed per request and duration, scale to zero, but have cold starts, time limits and no local state
A small team should lean on managed services (e.g. a managed database with automated backups and failover) to avoid operational burden
Trade-offs named: higher unit price, less control and vendor lock-in in exchange for less ops work

questions.prompt: A podcast app stores **40 TB** of audio and users download **300 TB per month**. Using **$0.023 per GB-month** for storage and **$0.09 per GB** for egress, estimate the monthly storage and bandwidth cost. What would you change?
keyPoints: Storage: 40,000 GB × $0.023 ≈ $920/month
Bandwidth is about 30x the storage cost and dominates the bill
Mitigations: serve through a CDN with lower negotiated per-GB rates and edge caching, compress or lower default bitrates, consider volume discounts or a cheaper-egress provider
questions.answer: Storage: `40,000 GB × 0.023 = $920`. Egress: `300,000 GB × 0.09 = $27,000`. Total ≈ **$28k/month**, about 97% of it bandwidth. Put a CDN in front (cheaper per GB, cached at the edge), use efficient audio encoding, and negotiate volume pricing.

questions.prompt: A function takes **100 ms** with **1 GB** of memory. Lambda-style pricing: **$0.20 per million requests** plus **$0.0000167 per GB-second**. A VM that can handle the load costs **$70/month**. At what average request rate does the VM become cheaper?
questions.hint: Find the cost per million requests first. A month is about 2.6 million seconds.
keyPoints: Compute per request: 0.1 s × 1 GB = 0.1 GB-s × $0.0000167 ≈ $0.00000167
Cost per million requests ≈ $1.67 + $0.20 = $1.87
Break-even: $70 / $1.87 ≈ 37 million requests per month
37M / ~2.6M seconds ≈ 14 requests per second on average; above that the VM is cheaper
Mentions that serverless still wins for spiky or near-zero traffic and saves ops effort
questions.answer: Per million: `1e6 × 0.1 × 1 × 0.0000167 = $1.67`, plus `$0.20` = **$1.87**. Break-even: `70 / 1.87 ≈ 37.4M` requests/month ≈ `37.4M / 2.63M s ≈ 14 req/s`. Above ~14 req/s sustained, the VM is cheaper (though you'd want two VMs for redundancy, moving break-even to ~28 req/s).

questions.prompt: Your nightly data-processing job runs on 50 on-demand VMs for 4 hours and costs a lot. Your manager asks you to cut the bill in half without making the job slower. What would you do?
questions.hint: Can this job tolerate being interrupted?
keyPoints: Batch jobs are a good fit for spot/preemptible instances, often 60–90% cheaper
Spot instances can be reclaimed with short notice, so the job must checkpoint progress and retry interrupted work idempotently
Diversify across instance types and AZs to reduce the chance of losing all capacity at once
Keep a small on-demand fallback or allow spot to be replaced by on-demand if capacity is unavailable
Also check right-sizing (are the VMs too big?) and data transfer costs

questions.prompt: Your e-commerce site runs in one region across three AZs. The CEO wants to survive a full region outage. Propose a multi-region design and explain its cost, RPO and RTO, and the hardest problem it introduces.
questions.hint: Active-passive or active-active? How does the database get to the other region?
keyPoints: Active-passive: a standby region with infrastructure ready (or scaled down) and DNS or global load balancer failover
Database replicated asynchronously across regions, so RPO is seconds of possibly lost writes; synchronous cross-region would add tens of ms to every write
RTO depends on automation: detecting the outage, promoting the replica, shifting traffic (minutes, if practiced regularly)
Cost roughly 1.5–2x plus cross-region data transfer
Active-active lowers latency for global users but must handle conflicting writes in two regions (e.g. partition users by home region or use conflict resolution)
Failover must be tested regularly or it will not work when needed
